back: The extent to which reports are compliant with standards, decision-useful (relevant and faithfully represented), complete, neutral and free from error.
Earnings are sustainable (will recur) and provide an adequate return, at least equal to the company's cost of capital.

front: Can a company have high reporting quality and low earnings quality?
back: Yes. For example, fully compliant statements that include a large one-time gain: the reporting is high quality, the earnings are not sustainable.
Aggressive: raises current earnings and assets, lowers future earnings. Conservative: lowers current earnings and assets, raises future earnings. Both are biases.
Motivation (pressure or incentive), opportunity (weak controls or oversight), rationalization (justifying the act).

front: What is a cookie jar reserve?
back: Over-accruing expenses or reserves in a strong year so they can be released in a weak year to smooth reported earnings.

front: Effect of capitalizing a cost instead of expensing it
back: Raises current pretax earnings and CFO (the outflow moves to investing), lowers earnings in later years through depreciation. Total cash is unchanged.

front: Days sales outstanding formula and warning sign
back: DSO = receivables / revenue x 365. A sharp rise while revenue grows suggests early recognition, loose credit or collectability problems.
(Total assets - cash and marketable securities) - (total liabilities - total debt).
(NOA end - NOA begin) / average NOA. Higher ratios suggest lower earnings quality.
(Net income - CFO - CFI) / average NOA, with CFI carried with its usual sign (negative when cash is spent). Higher ratios suggest lower earnings quality.
Receivables growing faster than revenue, a surge in last-quarter sales (channel stuffing), bill-and-hold sales, round-trip transactions and changes in recognition policy.
